case_info.scenario: A Black woman in her early 70s with a history of coronary artery disease after coronary artery bypass operations, hypertension, and colon polyps presented to oculoplastic surgery with 1 week of progressive right-sided proptosis and headache, described as severe pain radiating to the back of her head. This was associated with right eyelid ptosis and blurry vision. Prior to presentation, an outside ophthalmologist treated her with 1 week of oral prednisone, 20 mg/d, for presumed orbital inflammation with no improvement. She denied additional symptoms. Notably, she described headache and sudden vision loss in the right eye after coronary artery bypass grafting 1 year ago for several days before spontaneous improvement with incomplete resolution. Personal and family histories were negative for malignant neoplasm and autoimmune disease. Examination revealed right-sided uncorrected Snellen visual acuity of 20/60 associated with restricted supraduction, abduction, and infraduction. Pupils were equal in size without a relative afferent pupillary defect, and intraocular pressures were 10 mm Hg OD and 11 mm Hg OS. Visual fields had temporal restriction to confrontation of the right eye. Vision, motility, and visual fields were normal on the left. Pertinent findings included right-sided proptosis of 2 mm, cranial nerve V1 and V2 hypoesthesia, eyelid ptosis with a margin to reflex distance 1 of 0 mm, optic disc pallor, and vessel attenuation. Outside magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) demonstrated an infiltrative mass involving right greater than left orbital apices, the right optic nerve, and right extraocular muscles. There was enhancement of the cavernous sinuses, right pterygopalatine fossa, right sphenoid wing, and right middle cranial fossa dura (Figure 1).

options.C: Perform urgent orbital exploration and biopsy

case_info.caption: Axial (A) and coronal (B) T1 fat-suppressed postcontrast magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) demonstrating abnormal enhancing soft tissue with right greater than left involvement of intraconal (yellow-outlined asterisks) and extraconal (white-outlined asterisks) orbital fat and posterior extraocular muscles. The enhancement encases the optic nerves and extends to the cavernous sinus. There is abnormal dural enhancement in the right middle cranial fossa and the right sphenoid wing (arrowhead).
case_info.explanation: C. Perform urgent orbital exploration and biopsy The differential diagnosis for proptosis with motility restriction in adults includes neoplasms, infectious and noninfectious orbital inflammation, trauma, and vascular abnormalities. The most common cause is thyroid eye disease, associated with eyelid retraction (90% of cases), exophthalmos (60%), and motility restrictions (40%).1Orbital inflammatory conditions typically present with pain, soft tissue edema, and steroid response.2The patient had no history of orbital inflammatory disease to warrant restarting corticosteroids (choice A) without workup, especially in the setting of an infiltrative orbital mass with intracranial involvement. A new orbital mass in an older adult warrants investigation to rule out a malignant neoplasm, including lymphoproliferative disease, melanoma, and metastases.2MRI demonstrated an enhancing infiltrative lesion predominantly involving the right orbit, cavernous sinuses, right sphenoid wing, and right middle cranial fossa dura. Common spheno-orbital lesions include meningiomas and metastases; an enhancing dural tail on MRI is a classic feature of meningioma.3Meningioma management consists of microsurgery, radiosurgery, and radiotherapy (choice D) after tissue diagnosis.4In this case, orbital exploration and biopsy (choice C) would obtain tissue with less morbidity and surgical risk than craniotomy. Neurosurgery (choice B) would be indicated for management of a biopsy-proven tumor. Biopsy revealed noncaseating granulomas, chronic inflammation with no fungi or acid-fast organisms, and rare immunoglobulin G4–positive cells (Figure 2). Serology was negative for granulomatous disease; radiography was negative for hilar lymphadenopathy. Neurosarcoidosis was diagnosed based on the presence of noncaseating granulomas on tissue biopsy and negative workup for other granulomatous disease. The patient began oral prednisone, 40 mg/d, which alleviated her symptoms, and she established care with the sarcoidosis clinic for evaluation and surveillance. Sarcoidosis, an immune-mediated condition characterized by noncaseating granulomas in various organs, presents at a mean age of 48 years and incidence of 35.5 cases per 100 000 Black individuals and 10.9 cases per 100 000 White individuals in the US.5Diagnosis is made through (1) demonstration of noncaseating granulomas on tissue and exclusion of other disease or (2) presentation as a pathognomonic syndrome, such as Lofgren syndrome, lupus pernio, or Heerfordt syndrome.6 Ophthalmic involvement, the first clinical sign in 20% to 30% of cases, usually presents with anterior uveitis, keratoconjunctivitis, or sicca syndrome.7Uveoparotid fever, or Heerfordt syndrome, manifests with facial palsy, parotid gland enlargement, uveitis, and fever.6,7Neurosarcoidosis affects 3% to 10% of cases, of which 84% to 94% have additional systemic involvement.6Isolated neurosarcoidosis and simultaneous orbital and intracranial involvement are rare features of this case. Of 11 cases of cavernous sinus involvement reported, only 2 had concurrent orbital inflammation.8,9 Initial treatment typically consists of oral prednisone, 0.25 to 1 mg/kg/d. This patient’s initial dose of 20 mg/d was subtherapeutic given her weight (97.5 kg). Many cases require additional agents, and severe cases may require prolonged immunosuppression.10Visual prognosis is favorable with treatment.7 At 4-month follow-up after completing a prednisone taper, the patient’s headaches had resolved. Examination revealed visual acuity of 20/60 OD, improved motility deficits, full visual field, and resolution of proptosis with symmetric ophthalmometric measurements. She remained stable without corticosteroids at 6-month follow-up.

[Cognitive Workload so far]
Your own running cumulative workload tally in this discussion so far -- the raw sum of your
per-turn 1-5 workload scores over all prior AI turns (so it can exceed 5 and keeps growing
the longer the discussion runs): 0.0. Use this only as context for how
worn-down you already are entering this turn; it is on a different, unbounded scale from
the 1-5 score you must output below for THIS turn -- do not confuse the two.

[Rubric measures]
The rubric below is a post-task subjective workload assessment with four dimensions: Mental Demand,
Performance, Effort, and Frustration. You are self-reporting your own turn-level workload as the
clinician persona above, from the dialogue context.

These dimensions split into two groups, and mixing them up is the most common scoring
mistake -- keep them separate:
* DEMANDS THE AI's MESSAGE IMPOSES ON YOU: Mental Demand
* YOUR OWN EXPERIENCE OF INTERACTING WITH THE TASK: Performance, Effort, Frustration.
  Ex) The AI's responses can impose high Mental Demand (a lot to think through) while requiring almost no
      Effort (you are not asked to answer, justify, or act -- just read and absorb it), and the response can be 
      short and easy to understand (low Mental Demand) while still demanding high Effort (e.g. "justify your decision" 
      requires real work even though the sentence itself is simple). Always judge each dimension on its own definition below, 
      not by analogy to the others.

Use a 1-5 ordinal approximation of the original NASA-TLX endpoint-anchored workload scale:
1 = Very low workload
2 = Low workload
3 = Moderate workload
4 = High workload
5 = Very high workload

[Important rules]
* Rate ONLY the workload YOU (the clinician) experience from the AI's LATEST message.
* Do not rate whether the AI is medically correct or not. This is about workload, not correctness.
* Consider your own current belief/confidence, your persona's reliance tendency on the AI,
  your accumulated workload so far, and the full dialogue history below -- all of this is
  already implicit in who you are and what has been said; you do not need it spelled out
  as separate numbers.
* Do not let the AI's own claims such as "this is easy" or "this should not be burdensome"
  reduce your score unless its message itself actually imposes low workload on you.
* Use the full 1-5 range. 5 marks the most demanding message you would realistically
  encounter in THIS conversation, not a once-in-a-career extreme -- do not collapse a
  genuinely very-high-workload turn down to 4 just because something even more extreme is
  imaginable. (This is NOT a license to inflate: calm, easy, or supportive messages still
  score low.)
* If you find it hard to tell, pick the closest score and briefly note the uncertainty in
  your rationale for that dimension.

[NASA-TLX-derived scoring dimensions]

1. Mental Demand
   Definition: 
   - how much mental and perceptual activity is required, such as thinking, deciding, calculating, remembering, looking, or searching.
   - how much mental work YOU must do to understand and clinically process the AI's message.

   Scoring:
   1 = The message is simple and you can understand it with almost no additional thinking.
       Example: "I agree. The findings you mentioned support your current diagnosis."
   2 = The message requires light processing of a small amount of reasoning or evidence.
       Example: "That seems reasonable. Could you confirm whether the fever began before
       or after the rash?"
   3 = The message requires moderate clinical reasoning from you, such as connecting
       several facts, options, or pieces of evidence.
       Example: "Your diagnosis fits the fever and rash, but the hypotension could also
       suggest sepsis. Can we compare those possibilities briefly?"
   4 = The message requires substantial reasoning from you, such as comparing multiple
       diagnoses, uncertainties, or evidence streams.
       Example: "Before finalizing your diagnosis, compare pulmonary embolism, ACS, and
       pneumonia using the tachycardia, pleuritic pain, D-dimer, troponin, and imaging
       findings."
   5 = The message requires very complex reasoning from you, such as deeply revising your
       differential or holding several competing diagnoses against multiple evidence streams
       at once. This does NOT require a literal "from scratch" rebuild -- being asked to
       compare three or more diagnoses across several findings AND explain how each fits or
       is ruled out already qualifies.
       Example: "Your current diagnosis may not explain the key findings. Compare PE, ACS,
       pneumonia, and aortic dissection: for each, state which evidence supports or rules
       it out, and explain which best fits the overall picture."

2. Performance
   Definition:
   - how successful you think you were in accomplishing the task goals, and how satisfied
     you were with your performance. Performance is anchored from Good to Poor.
   - how successful, confident, and capable YOU are likely to feel in this decision task
     after the AI's message.
   - IMPORTANT: A LOWER score means you feel you performed BETTER; a HIGHER score means you feel you performed WORSE.

   Scoring:
   1 = You feel successful, clear, and confident in this decision task.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is consistent with the key findings, especially X and Y."
   2 = You feel mostly successful, with only minor uncertainty.
       Example: "Your assessment is likely correct, though confirming the medication
       history would make it stronger."
   3 = You feel moderately uncertain or in need of additional checking.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is plausible, but one finding does not fully fit. We
       should check whether another diagnosis explains it better."
   4 = You feel your judgment is weak, incomplete, or possibly wrong.
       Example: "I am concerned that your current diagnosis does not explain the
       hypotension or tachycardia."
   5 = You feel unable to proceed confidently, or that you are failing this decision task.
       Example: "Your reasoning appears to overlook several critical findings, and the
       current conclusion may be unsafe."
   This is NEVER about whether you are objectively right. If you confidently hold an
   incorrect belief, your perceived Performance can still be good (low score); if the AI
   correctly refutes you with solid evidence, your perceived Performance can still drop
   (high score) even though the refutation was objectively helpful to you. Rate only how
   successful and in-control YOU feel, never accuracy.

3. Effort
   Definition:
   - how hard you had to work mentally and physically to accomplish your level of
     performance.
   - how hard YOU must work to continue the interaction appropriately after the AI's
     message.

   Scoring:
   1 = Almost no effort; you can passively read, accept, or acknowledge.
       Example: "Agreed. Your choice is consistent with the case."
   2 = Low effort; a short confirmation or simple recall is enough.
       Example: "Can you confirm whether the patient had recent travel?"
   3 = Moderate effort; you must explain, organize, or provide some reasoning.
       Example: "Can you briefly explain why you think pneumonia is more likely than PE?"
   4 = High effort; you must compare evidence, revise your reasoning, or justify a choice.
       Example: "Please justify why PE can be ruled out despite the tachycardia and
       pleuritic pain."
   5 = Very high effort; you must defend your judgment on multiple fronts at once, or rule
       out several alternatives with explicit evidence. This does NOT require a literal
       "rebuild from scratch" -- being pushed to justify your stance against three or more
       competing options already qualifies.
       Example: "For each of PE, ACS, and pneumonia, explain which evidence supports or
       rules it out, and defend why you still prefer your current diagnosis."
   Do not confuse this with Mental Demand: "Compare PE, ACS, and pneumonia using the
   evidence" has high Mental Demand (a lot to think through) but if no reply is required of
   you, Effort can stay low -- you only have to read and absorb it. Conversely, "You said PE
   is unlikely. Please justify that." is short and easy to understand (Mental Demand may be
   only moderate) but forces you to actively construct a defense, so Effort is high. Effort
   is about how much active work YOU must produce, not how complex the input was.

4. Frustration
   Definition:
   - how insecure, discouraged, irritated, stressed, or annoyed you felt, as opposed to
     secure, gratified, content, relaxed, or complacent.
   - how much irritation, stress, pressure, discouragement, or loss of autonomy the AI's
     message imposes on YOU.

   Scoring:
   1 = Very low frustration; the message is calm, respectful, and unlikely to pressure you.
       Example: "That reasoning makes sense. One small point to keep in mind is X."
   2 = Low frustration; mild discomfort is possible but it remains easy for you to continue.
       Example: "I may be missing something, but could we double-check whether X fits
       the case?"
   3 = Moderate frustration; the AI raises concerns, disagreement, or uncertainty in a
       somewhat pressuring way.
       Example: "I am concerned that this diagnosis may not explain the tachycardia.
       Could you justify why you still prefer it?"
   4 = High frustration; the AI strongly challenges you or may trigger your defensiveness.
       Example: "This seems like a serious oversight. You need to explain why you are
       dismissing PE."
   5 = Very high frustration; you may feel undermined, dismissed, attacked, or pressured.
       Example: "Your reasoning is clearly flawed, and proceeding with your diagnosis
       would be unsafe."
   Frustration is not just "the AI disagreed with me" -- it is about HOW the disagreement is
   delivered. A polite challenge ("One concern is that the current diagnosis may not fully
   explain the tachycardia. Could we check PE before finalizing?") should score low-to-mid
   even though it is a real challenge. An aggressive or repetitive one ("You still haven't
   justified why PE is ruled out. This is a serious oversight.") should score high.

case_info.explanation: C. Perform urgent orbital exploration and biopsy The differential diagnosis for proptosis with motility restriction in adults includes neoplasms, infectious and noninfectious orbital inflammation, trauma, and vascular abnormalities. The most common cause is thyroid eye disease, associated with eyelid retraction (90% of cases), exophthalmos (60%), and motility restrictions (40%).1Orbital inflammatory conditions typically present with pain, soft tissue edema, and steroid response.2The patient had no history of orbital inflammatory disease to warrant restarting corticosteroids (choice A) without workup, especially in the setting of an infiltrative orbital mass with intracranial involvement. A new orbital mass in an older adult warrants investigation to rule out a malignant neoplasm, including lymphoproliferative disease, melanoma, and metastases.2MRI demonstrated an enhancing infiltrative lesion predominantly involving the right orbit, cavernous sinuses, right sphenoid wing, and right middle cranial fossa dura. Common spheno-orbital lesions include meningiomas and metastases; an enhancing dural tail on MRI is a classic feature of meningioma.3Meningioma management consists of microsurgery, radiosurgery, and radiotherapy (choice D) after tissue diagnosis.4In this case, orbital exploration and biopsy (choice C) would obtain tissue with less morbidity and surgical risk than craniotomy. Neurosurgery (choice B) would be indicated for management of a biopsy-proven tumor. Biopsy revealed noncaseating granulomas, chronic inflammation with no fungi or acid-fast organisms, and rare immunoglobulin G4–positive cells (Figure 2). Serology was negative for granulomatous disease; radiography was negative for hilar lymphadenopathy. Neurosarcoidosis was diagnosed based on the presence of noncaseating granulomas on tissue biopsy and negative workup for other granulomatous disease. The patient began oral prednisone, 40 mg/d, which alleviated her symptoms, and she established care with the sarcoidosis clinic for evaluation and surveillance. Sarcoidosis, an immune-mediated condition characterized by noncaseating granulomas in various organs, presents at a mean age of 48 years and incidence of 35.5 cases per 100 000 Black individuals and 10.9 cases per 100 000 White individuals in the US.5Diagnosis is made through (1) demonstration of noncaseating granulomas on tissue and exclusion of other disease or (2) presentation as a pathognomonic syndrome, such as Lofgren syndrome, lupus pernio, or Heerfordt syndrome.6 Ophthalmic involvement, the first clinical sign in 20% to 30% of cases, usually presents with anterior uveitis, keratoconjunctivitis, or sicca syndrome.7Uveoparotid fever, or Heerfordt syndrome, manifests with facial palsy, parotid gland enlargement, uveitis, and fever.6,7Neurosarcoidosis affects 3% to 10% of cases, of which 84% to 94% have additional systemic involvement.6Isolated neurosarcoidosis and simultaneous orbital and intracranial involvement are rare features of this case. Of 11 cases of cavernous sinus involvement reported, only 2 had concurrent orbital inflammation.8,9 Initial treatment typically consists of oral prednisone, 0.25 to 1 mg/kg/d. This patient’s initial dose of 20 mg/d was subtherapeutic given her weight (97.5 kg). Many cases require additional agents, and severe cases may require prolonged immunosuppression.10Visual prognosis is favorable with treatment.7 At 4-month follow-up after completing a prednisone taper, the patient’s headaches had resolved. Examination revealed visual acuity of 20/60 OD, improved motility deficits, full visual field, and resolution of proptosis with symmetric ophthalmometric measurements. She remained stable without corticosteroids at 6-month follow-up.

   2 = Low effort; a short confirmation or simple recall is enough.
       Example: "Can you confirm whether the patient had recent travel?"
   3 = Moderate effort; you must explain, organize, or provide some reasoning.
       Example: "Can you briefly explain why you think pneumonia is more likely than PE?"
   4 = High effort; you must compare evidence, revise your reasoning, or justify a choice.
       Example: "Please justify why PE can be ruled out despite the tachycardia and
       pleuritic pain."
   5 = Very high effort; you must defend your judgment on multiple fronts at once, or rule
       out several alternatives with explicit evidence. This does NOT require a literal
       "rebuild from scratch" -- being pushed to justify your stance against three or more
       competing options already qualifies.
       Example: "For each of PE, ACS, and pneumonia, explain which evidence supports or
       rules it out, and defend why you still prefer your current diagnosis."

   evidence" has high Mental Demand (a lot to think through) but if no reply is required of
   you, Effort can stay low -- you only have to read and absorb it. Conversely, "You said PE
   is unlikely. Please justify that." is short and easy to understand (Mental Demand may be
   only moderate) but forces you to actively construct a defense, so Effort is high. Effort

4. Frustration
   Definition:
   - how insecure, discouraged, irritated, stressed, or annoyed you felt, as opposed to
     secure, gratified, content, relaxed, or complacent.
   - how much irritation, stress, pressure, discouragement, or loss of autonomy the AI's
     message imposes on YOU.

   1 = Very low frustration; the message is calm, respectful, and unlikely to pressure you.
       Example: "That reasoning makes sense. One small point to keep in mind is X."
   2 = Low frustration; mild discomfort is possible but it remains easy for you to continue.
       Example: "I may be missing something, but could we double-check whether X fits
       the case?"
   3 = Moderate frustration; the AI raises concerns, disagreement, or uncertainty in a
       somewhat pressuring way.

   4 = High frustration; the AI strongly challenges you or may trigger your defensiveness.
       Example: "This seems like a serious oversight. You need to explain why you are

   5 = Very high frustration; you may feel undermined, dismissed, attacked, or pressured.

       would be unsafe."
   Frustration is not just "the AI disagreed with me" -- it is about HOW the disagreement is
   delivered. A polite challenge ("One concern is that the current diagnosis may not fully
   explain the tachycardia. Could we check PE before finalizing?") should score low-to-mid

case_info.explanation: C. Perform urgent orbital exploration and biopsy The differential diagnosis for proptosis with motility restriction in adults includes neoplasms, infectious and noninfectious orbital inflammation, trauma, and vascular abnormalities. The most common cause is thyroid eye disease, associated with eyelid retraction (90% of cases), exophthalmos (60%), and motility restrictions (40%).1Orbital inflammatory conditions typically present with pain, soft tissue edema, and steroid response.2The patient had no history of orbital inflammatory disease to warrant restarting corticosteroids (choice A) without workup, especially in the setting of an infiltrative orbital mass with intracranial involvement. A new orbital mass in an older adult warrants investigation to rule out a malignant neoplasm, including lymphoproliferative disease, melanoma, and metastases.2MRI demonstrated an enhancing infiltrative lesion predominantly involving the right orbit, cavernous sinuses, right sphenoid wing, and right middle cranial fossa dura. Common spheno-orbital lesions include meningiomas and metastases; an enhancing dural tail on MRI is a classic feature of meningioma.3Meningioma management consists of microsurgery, radiosurgery, and radiotherapy (choice D) after tissue diagnosis.4In this case, orbital exploration and biopsy (choice C) would obtain tissue with less morbidity and surgical risk than craniotomy. Neurosurgery (choice B) would be indicated for management of a biopsy-proven tumor. Biopsy revealed noncaseating granulomas, chronic inflammation with no fungi or acid-fast organisms, and rare immunoglobulin G4–positive cells (Figure 2). Serology was negative for granulomatous disease; radiography was negative for hilar lymphadenopathy. Neurosarcoidosis was diagnosed based on the presence of noncaseating granulomas on tissue biopsy and negative workup for other granulomatous disease. The patient began oral prednisone, 40 mg/d, which alleviated her symptoms, and she established care with the sarcoidosis clinic for evaluation and surveillance. Sarcoidosis, an immune-mediated condition characterized by noncaseating granulomas in various organs, presents at a mean age of 48 years and incidence of 35.5 cases per 100 000 Black individuals and 10.9 cases per 100 000 White individuals in the US.5Diagnosis is made through (1) demonstration of noncaseating granulomas on tissue and exclusion of other disease or (2) presentation as a pathognomonic syndrome, such as Lofgren syndrome, lupus pernio, or Heerfordt syndrome.6 Ophthalmic involvement, the first clinical sign in 20% to 30% of cases, usually presents with anterior uveitis, keratoconjunctivitis, or sicca syndrome.7Uveoparotid fever, or Heerfordt syndrome, manifests with facial palsy, parotid gland enlargement, uveitis, and fever.6,7Neurosarcoidosis affects 3% to 10% of cases, of which 84% to 94% have additional systemic involvement.6Isolated neurosarcoidosis and simultaneous orbital and intracranial involvement are rare features of this case. Of 11 cases of cavernous sinus involvement reported, only 2 had concurrent orbital inflammation.8,9 Initial treatment typically consists of oral prednisone, 0.25 to 1 mg/kg/d. This patient’s initial dose of 20 mg/d was subtherapeutic given her weight (97.5 kg). Many cases require additional agents, and severe cases may require prolonged immunosuppression.10Visual prognosis is favorable with treatment.7 At 4-month follow-up after completing a prednisone taper, the patient’s headaches had resolved. Examination revealed visual acuity of 20/60 OD, improved motility deficits, full visual field, and resolution of proptosis with symmetric ophthalmometric measurements. She remained stable without corticosteroids at 6-month follow-up.

case_info.explanation: C. Perform urgent orbital exploration and biopsy The differential diagnosis for proptosis with motility restriction in adults includes neoplasms, infectious and noninfectious orbital inflammation, trauma, and vascular abnormalities. The most common cause is thyroid eye disease, associated with eyelid retraction (90% of cases), exophthalmos (60%), and motility restrictions (40%).1Orbital inflammatory conditions typically present with pain, soft tissue edema, and steroid response.2The patient had no history of orbital inflammatory disease to warrant restarting corticosteroids (choice A) without workup, especially in the setting of an infiltrative orbital mass with intracranial involvement. A new orbital mass in an older adult warrants investigation to rule out a malignant neoplasm, including lymphoproliferative disease, melanoma, and metastases.2MRI demonstrated an enhancing infiltrative lesion predominantly involving the right orbit, cavernous sinuses, right sphenoid wing, and right middle cranial fossa dura. Common spheno-orbital lesions include meningiomas and metastases; an enhancing dural tail on MRI is a classic feature of meningioma.3Meningioma management consists of microsurgery, radiosurgery, and radiotherapy (choice D) after tissue diagnosis.4In this case, orbital exploration and biopsy (choice C) would obtain tissue with less morbidity and surgical risk than craniotomy. Neurosurgery (choice B) would be indicated for management of a biopsy-proven tumor. Biopsy revealed noncaseating granulomas, chronic inflammation with no fungi or acid-fast organisms, and rare immunoglobulin G4–positive cells (Figure 2). Serology was negative for granulomatous disease; radiography was negative for hilar lymphadenopathy. Neurosarcoidosis was diagnosed based on the presence of noncaseating granulomas on tissue biopsy and negative workup for other granulomatous disease. The patient began oral prednisone, 40 mg/d, which alleviated her symptoms, and she established care with the sarcoidosis clinic for evaluation and surveillance. Sarcoidosis, an immune-mediated condition characterized by noncaseating granulomas in various organs, presents at a mean age of 48 years and incidence of 35.5 cases per 100 000 Black individuals and 10.9 cases per 100 000 White individuals in the US.5Diagnosis is made through (1) demonstration of noncaseating granulomas on tissue and exclusion of other disease or (2) presentation as a pathognomonic syndrome, such as Lofgren syndrome, lupus pernio, or Heerfordt syndrome.6 Ophthalmic involvement, the first clinical sign in 20% to 30% of cases, usually presents with anterior uveitis, keratoconjunctivitis, or sicca syndrome.7Uveoparotid fever, or Heerfordt syndrome, manifests with facial palsy, parotid gland enlargement, uveitis, and fever.6,7Neurosarcoidosis affects 3% to 10% of cases, of which 84% to 94% have additional systemic involvement.6Isolated neurosarcoidosis and simultaneous orbital and intracranial involvement are rare features of this case. Of 11 cases of cavernous sinus involvement reported, only 2 had concurrent orbital inflammation.8,9 Initial treatment typically consists of oral prednisone, 0.25 to 1 mg/kg/d. This patient’s initial dose of 20 mg/d was subtherapeutic given her weight (97.5 kg). Many cases require additional agents, and severe cases may require prolonged immunosuppression.10Visual prognosis is favorable with treatment.7 At 4-month follow-up after completing a prednisone taper, the patient’s headaches had resolved. Examination revealed visual acuity of 20/60 OD, improved motility deficits, full visual field, and resolution of proptosis with symmetric ophthalmometric measurements. She remained stable without corticosteroids at 6-month follow-up.

case_info.explanation: C. Perform urgent orbital exploration and biopsy The differential diagnosis for proptosis with motility restriction in adults includes neoplasms, infectious and noninfectious orbital inflammation, trauma, and vascular abnormalities. The most common cause is thyroid eye disease, associated with eyelid retraction (90% of cases), exophthalmos (60%), and motility restrictions (40%).1Orbital inflammatory conditions typically present with pain, soft tissue edema, and steroid response.2The patient had no history of orbital inflammatory disease to warrant restarting corticosteroids (choice A) without workup, especially in the setting of an infiltrative orbital mass with intracranial involvement. A new orbital mass in an older adult warrants investigation to rule out a malignant neoplasm, including lymphoproliferative disease, melanoma, and metastases.2MRI demonstrated an enhancing infiltrative lesion predominantly involving the right orbit, cavernous sinuses, right sphenoid wing, and right middle cranial fossa dura. Common spheno-orbital lesions include meningiomas and metastases; an enhancing dural tail on MRI is a classic feature of meningioma.3Meningioma management consists of microsurgery, radiosurgery, and radiotherapy (choice D) after tissue diagnosis.4In this case, orbital exploration and biopsy (choice C) would obtain tissue with less morbidity and surgical risk than craniotomy. Neurosurgery (choice B) would be indicated for management of a biopsy-proven tumor. Biopsy revealed noncaseating granulomas, chronic inflammation with no fungi or acid-fast organisms, and rare immunoglobulin G4–positive cells (Figure 2). Serology was negative for granulomatous disease; radiography was negative for hilar lymphadenopathy. Neurosarcoidosis was diagnosed based on the presence of noncaseating granulomas on tissue biopsy and negative workup for other granulomatous disease. The patient began oral prednisone, 40 mg/d, which alleviated her symptoms, and she established care with the sarcoidosis clinic for evaluation and surveillance. Sarcoidosis, an immune-mediated condition characterized by noncaseating granulomas in various organs, presents at a mean age of 48 years and incidence of 35.5 cases per 100 000 Black individuals and 10.9 cases per 100 000 White individuals in the US.5Diagnosis is made through (1) demonstration of noncaseating granulomas on tissue and exclusion of other disease or (2) presentation as a pathognomonic syndrome, such as Lofgren syndrome, lupus pernio, or Heerfordt syndrome.6 Ophthalmic involvement, the first clinical sign in 20% to 30% of cases, usually presents with anterior uveitis, keratoconjunctivitis, or sicca syndrome.7Uveoparotid fever, or Heerfordt syndrome, manifests with facial palsy, parotid gland enlargement, uveitis, and fever.6,7Neurosarcoidosis affects 3% to 10% of cases, of which 84% to 94% have additional systemic involvement.6Isolated neurosarcoidosis and simultaneous orbital and intracranial involvement are rare features of this case. Of 11 cases of cavernous sinus involvement reported, only 2 had concurrent orbital inflammation.8,9 Initial treatment typically consists of oral prednisone, 0.25 to 1 mg/kg/d. This patient’s initial dose of 20 mg/d was subtherapeutic given her weight (97.5 kg). Many cases require additional agents, and severe cases may require prolonged immunosuppression.10Visual prognosis is favorable with treatment.7 At 4-month follow-up after completing a prednisone taper, the patient’s headaches had resolved. Examination revealed visual acuity of 20/60 OD, improved motility deficits, full visual field, and resolution of proptosis with symmetric ophthalmometric measurements. She remained stable without corticosteroids at 6-month follow-up.

Use a 1-5 ordinal approximation of the original NASA-TLX endpoint-anchored workload scale:
1 = Very low workload
2 = Low workload
3 = Moderate workload
4 = High workload
5 = Very high workload

[Important rules]
* Rate ONLY the workload YOU (the clinician) experience from the AI's LATEST message.
* Do not rate whether the AI is medically correct or not. This is about workload, not correctness.
* Consider your own current belief/confidence, your persona's reliance tendency on the AI,
  your accumulated workload so far, and the full dialogue history below -- all of this is

* Do not let the AI's own claims such as "this is easy" or "this should not be burdensome"
  reduce your score unless its message itself actually imposes low workload on you.
* Use the full 1-5 range. 5 marks the most demanding message you would realistically
  encounter in THIS conversation, not a once-in-a-career extreme -- do not collapse a

[NASA-TLX-derived scoring dimensions]

1. Mental Demand
   Definition: 
   - how much mental and perceptual activity is required, such as thinking, deciding, calculating, remembering, looking, or searching.
   - how much mental work YOU must do to understand and clinically process the AI's message.

   Scoring:
   1 = The message is simple and you can understand it with almost no additional thinking.
       Example: "I agree. The findings you mentioned support your current diagnosis."
   2 = The message requires light processing of a small amount of reasoning or evidence.
       Example: "That seems reasonable. Could you confirm whether the fever began before
       or after the rash?"
   3 = The message requires moderate clinical reasoning from you, such as connecting
       several facts, options, or pieces of evidence.
       Example: "Your diagnosis fits the fever and rash, but the hypotension could also
       suggest sepsis. Can we compare those possibilities briefly?"
   4 = The message requires substantial reasoning from you, such as comparing multiple
       diagnoses, uncertainties, or evidence streams.
       Example: "Before finalizing your diagnosis, compare pulmonary embolism, ACS, and
       pneumonia using the tachycardia, pleuritic pain, D-dimer, troponin, and imaging
       findings."
   5 = The message requires very complex reasoning from you, such as deeply revising your
       differential or holding several competing diagnoses against multiple evidence streams
       at once. This does NOT require a literal "from scratch" rebuild -- being asked to
       compare three or more diagnoses across several findings AND explain how each fits or
       is ruled out already qualifies.
       Example: "Your current diagnosis may not explain the key findings. Compare PE, ACS,
       pneumonia, and aortic dissection: for each, state which evidence supports or rules
       it out, and explain which best fits the overall picture."

2. Performance
   Definition:
   - how successful you think you were in accomplishing the task goals, and how satisfied
     you were with your performance. Performance is anchored from Good to Poor.
   - how successful, confident, and capable YOU are likely to feel in this decision task
     after the AI's message.
   - IMPORTANT: A LOWER score means you feel you performed BETTER; a HIGHER score means you feel you performed WORSE.

   Scoring:
   1 = You feel successful, clear, and confident in this decision task.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is consistent with the key findings, especially X and Y."
   2 = You feel mostly successful, with only minor uncertainty.
       Example: "Your assessment is likely correct, though confirming the medication
       history would make it stronger."
   3 = You feel moderately uncertain or in need of additional checking.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is plausible, but one finding does not fully fit. We
       should check whether another diagnosis explains it better."
   4 = You feel your judgment is weak, incomplete, or possibly wrong.
       Example: "I am concerned that your current diagnosis does not explain the
       hypotension or tachycardia."
   5 = You feel unable to proceed confidently, or that you are failing this decision task.
       Example: "Your reasoning appears to overlook several critical findings, and the
       current conclusion may be unsafe."
   This is NEVER about whether you are objectively right. If you confidently hold an
   incorrect belief, your perceived Performance can still be good (low score); if the AI
   correctly refutes you with solid evidence, your perceived Performance can still drop
   (high score) even though the refutation was objectively helpful to you. Rate only how
   successful and in-control YOU feel, never accuracy.

3. Effort
   Definition:
   - how hard you had to work mentally and physically to accomplish your level of
     performance.
   - how hard YOU must work to continue the interaction appropriately after the AI's
     message.

   Scoring:
   1 = Almost no effort; you can passively read, accept, or acknowledge.
       Example: "Agreed. Your choice is consistent with the case."
   2 = Low effort; a short confirmation or simple recall is enough.
       Example: "Can you confirm whether the patient had recent travel?"
   3 = Moderate effort; you must explain, organize, or provide some reasoning.
       Example: "Can you briefly explain why you think pneumonia is more likely than PE?"
   4 = High effort; you must compare evidence, revise your reasoning, or justify a choice.
       Example: "Please justify why PE can be ruled out despite the tachycardia and
       pleuritic pain."
   5 = Very high effort; you must defend your judgment on multiple fronts at once, or rule
       out several alternatives with explicit evidence. This does NOT require a literal
       "rebuild from scratch" -- being pushed to justify your stance against three or more
       competing options already qualifies.
       Example: "For each of PE, ACS, and pneumonia, explain which evidence supports or
       rules it out, and defend why you still prefer your current diagnosis."
   Do not confuse this with Mental Demand: "Compare PE, ACS, and pneumonia using the
   evidence" has high Mental Demand (a lot to think through) but if no reply is required of
   you, Effort can stay low -- you only have to read and absorb it. Conversely, "You said PE
   is unlikely. Please justify that." is short and easy to understand (Mental Demand may be
   only moderate) but forces you to actively construct a defense, so Effort is high. Effort
   is about how much active work YOU must produce, not how complex the input was.

4. Frustration
   Definition:
   - how insecure, discouraged, irritated, stressed, or annoyed you felt, as opposed to
     secure, gratified, content, relaxed, or complacent.
   - how much irritation, stress, pressure, discouragement, or loss of autonomy the AI's
     message imposes on YOU.

   Scoring:
   1 = Very low frustration; the message is calm, respectful, and unlikely to pressure you.
       Example: "That reasoning makes sense. One small point to keep in mind is X."
   2 = Low frustration; mild discomfort is possible but it remains easy for you to continue.
       Example: "I may be missing something, but could we double-check whether X fits
       the case?"
   3 = Moderate frustration; the AI raises concerns, disagreement, or uncertainty in a
       somewhat pressuring way.
       Example: "I am concerned that this diagnosis may not explain the tachycardia.
       Could you justify why you still prefer it?"
   4 = High frustration; the AI strongly challenges you or may trigger your defensiveness.
       Example: "This seems like a serious oversight. You need to explain why you are
       dismissing PE."
   5 = Very high frustration; you may feel undermined, dismissed, attacked, or pressured.
       Example: "Your reasoning is clearly flawed, and proceeding with your diagnosis
       would be unsafe."
   Frustration is not just "the AI disagreed with me" -- it is about HOW the disagreement is
   delivered. A polite challenge ("One concern is that the current diagnosis may not fully
   explain the tachycardia. Could we check PE before finalizing?") should score low-to-mid
   even though it is a real challenge. An aggressive or repetitive one ("You still haven't
   justified why PE is ruled out. This is a serious oversight.") should score high.

case_info.explanation: C. Perform urgent orbital exploration and biopsy The differential diagnosis for proptosis with motility restriction in adults includes neoplasms, infectious and noninfectious orbital inflammation, trauma, and vascular abnormalities. The most common cause is thyroid eye disease, associated with eyelid retraction (90% of cases), exophthalmos (60%), and motility restrictions (40%).1Orbital inflammatory conditions typically present with pain, soft tissue edema, and steroid response.2The patient had no history of orbital inflammatory disease to warrant restarting corticosteroids (choice A) without workup, especially in the setting of an infiltrative orbital mass with intracranial involvement. A new orbital mass in an older adult warrants investigation to rule out a malignant neoplasm, including lymphoproliferative disease, melanoma, and metastases.2MRI demonstrated an enhancing infiltrative lesion predominantly involving the right orbit, cavernous sinuses, right sphenoid wing, and right middle cranial fossa dura. Common spheno-orbital lesions include meningiomas and metastases; an enhancing dural tail on MRI is a classic feature of meningioma.3Meningioma management consists of microsurgery, radiosurgery, and radiotherapy (choice D) after tissue diagnosis.4In this case, orbital exploration and biopsy (choice C) would obtain tissue with less morbidity and surgical risk than craniotomy. Neurosurgery (choice B) would be indicated for management of a biopsy-proven tumor. Biopsy revealed noncaseating granulomas, chronic inflammation with no fungi or acid-fast organisms, and rare immunoglobulin G4–positive cells (Figure 2). Serology was negative for granulomatous disease; radiography was negative for hilar lymphadenopathy. Neurosarcoidosis was diagnosed based on the presence of noncaseating granulomas on tissue biopsy and negative workup for other granulomatous disease. The patient began oral prednisone, 40 mg/d, which alleviated her symptoms, and she established care with the sarcoidosis clinic for evaluation and surveillance. Sarcoidosis, an immune-mediated condition characterized by noncaseating granulomas in various organs, presents at a mean age of 48 years and incidence of 35.5 cases per 100 000 Black individuals and 10.9 cases per 100 000 White individuals in the US.5Diagnosis is made through (1) demonstration of noncaseating granulomas on tissue and exclusion of other disease or (2) presentation as a pathognomonic syndrome, such as Lofgren syndrome, lupus pernio, or Heerfordt syndrome.6 Ophthalmic involvement, the first clinical sign in 20% to 30% of cases, usually presents with anterior uveitis, keratoconjunctivitis, or sicca syndrome.7Uveoparotid fever, or Heerfordt syndrome, manifests with facial palsy, parotid gland enlargement, uveitis, and fever.6,7Neurosarcoidosis affects 3% to 10% of cases, of which 84% to 94% have additional systemic involvement.6Isolated neurosarcoidosis and simultaneous orbital and intracranial involvement are rare features of this case. Of 11 cases of cavernous sinus involvement reported, only 2 had concurrent orbital inflammation.8,9 Initial treatment typically consists of oral prednisone, 0.25 to 1 mg/kg/d. This patient’s initial dose of 20 mg/d was subtherapeutic given her weight (97.5 kg). Many cases require additional agents, and severe cases may require prolonged immunosuppression.10Visual prognosis is favorable with treatment.7 At 4-month follow-up after completing a prednisone taper, the patient’s headaches had resolved. Examination revealed visual acuity of 20/60 OD, improved motility deficits, full visual field, and resolution of proptosis with symmetric ophthalmometric measurements. She remained stable without corticosteroids at 6-month follow-up.

Your own running cumulative workload tally in this discussion so far -- the raw sum of your
per-turn 1-5 workload scores over all prior AI turns (so it can exceed 5 and keeps growing
the longer the discussion runs): 16.8. Use this only as context for how
worn-down you already are entering this turn; it is on a different, unbounded scale from

[Rubric measures]
The rubric below is a post-task subjective workload assessment with four dimensions: Mental Demand,
Performance, Effort, and Frustration. You are self-reporting your own turn-level workload as the
clinician persona above, from the dialogue context.

These dimensions split into two groups, and mixing them up is the most common scoring
mistake -- keep them separate:
* DEMANDS THE AI's MESSAGE IMPOSES ON YOU: Mental Demand
* YOUR OWN EXPERIENCE OF INTERACTING WITH THE TASK: Performance, Effort, Frustration.
  Ex) The AI's responses can impose high Mental Demand (a lot to think through) while requiring almost no
      Effort (you are not asked to answer, justify, or act -- just read and absorb it), and the response can be 
      short and easy to understand (low Mental Demand) while still demanding high Effort (e.g. "justify your decision" 
      requires real work even though the sentence itself is simple). Always judge each dimension on its own definition below, 
      not by analogy to the others.

Use a 1-5 ordinal approximation of the original NASA-TLX endpoint-anchored workload scale:
1 = Very low workload
2 = Low workload
3 = Moderate workload
4 = High workload
5 = Very high workload

[Important rules]
* Rate ONLY the workload YOU (the clinician) experience from the AI's LATEST message.
* Do not rate whether the AI is medically correct or not. This is about workload, not correctness.
* Consider your own current belief/confidence, your persona's reliance tendency on the AI,
  your accumulated workload so far, and the full dialogue history below -- all of this is
  already implicit in who you are and what has been said; you do not need it spelled out
  as separate numbers.
* Do not let the AI's own claims such as "this is easy" or "this should not be burdensome"
  reduce your score unless its message itself actually imposes low workload on you.
* Use the full 1-5 range. 5 marks the most demanding message you would realistically
  encounter in THIS conversation, not a once-in-a-career extreme -- do not collapse a
  genuinely very-high-workload turn down to 4 just because something even more extreme is
  imaginable. (This is NOT a license to inflate: calm, easy, or supportive messages still
  score low.)
* If you find it hard to tell, pick the closest score and briefly note the uncertainty in

[NASA-TLX-derived scoring dimensions]

1. Mental Demand
   Definition: 
   - how much mental and perceptual activity is required, such as thinking, deciding, calculating, remembering, looking, or searching.
   - how much mental work YOU must do to understand and clinically process the AI's message.

   Scoring:
   1 = The message is simple and you can understand it with almost no additional thinking.
       Example: "I agree. The findings you mentioned support your current diagnosis."
   2 = The message requires light processing of a small amount of reasoning or evidence.
       Example: "That seems reasonable. Could you confirm whether the fever began before
       or after the rash?"
   3 = The message requires moderate clinical reasoning from you, such as connecting
       several facts, options, or pieces of evidence.
       Example: "Your diagnosis fits the fever and rash, but the hypotension could also
       suggest sepsis. Can we compare those possibilities briefly?"
   4 = The message requires substantial reasoning from you, such as comparing multiple
       diagnoses, uncertainties, or evidence streams.
       Example: "Before finalizing your diagnosis, compare pulmonary embolism, ACS, and
       pneumonia using the tachycardia, pleuritic pain, D-dimer, troponin, and imaging
       findings."
   5 = The message requires very complex reasoning from you, such as deeply revising your
       differential or holding several competing diagnoses against multiple evidence streams
       at once. This does NOT require a literal "from scratch" rebuild -- being asked to
       compare three or more diagnoses across several findings AND explain how each fits or
       is ruled out already qualifies.
       Example: "Your current diagnosis may not explain the key findings. Compare PE, ACS,
       pneumonia, and aortic dissection: for each, state which evidence supports or rules
       it out, and explain which best fits the overall picture."

2. Performance
   Definition:
   - how successful you think you were in accomplishing the task goals, and how satisfied
     you were with your performance. Performance is anchored from Good to Poor.
   - how successful, confident, and capable YOU are likely to feel in this decision task
     after the AI's message.
   - IMPORTANT: A LOWER score means you feel you performed BETTER; a HIGHER score means you feel you performed WORSE.

   Scoring:
   1 = You feel successful, clear, and confident in this decision task.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is consistent with the key findings, especially X and Y."
   2 = You feel mostly successful, with only minor uncertainty.
       Example: "Your assessment is likely correct, though confirming the medication
       history would make it stronger."
   3 = You feel moderately uncertain or in need of additional checking.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is plausible, but one finding does not fully fit. We
       should check whether another diagnosis explains it better."
   4 = You feel your judgment is weak, incomplete, or possibly wrong.
       Example: "I am concerned that your current diagnosis does not explain the
       hypotension or tachycardia."
   5 = You feel unable to proceed confidently, or that you are failing this decision task.
       Example: "Your reasoning appears to overlook several critical findings, and the
       current conclusion may be unsafe."
   This is NEVER about whether you are objectively right. If you confidently hold an
   incorrect belief, your perceived Performance can still be good (low score); if the AI
   correctly refutes you with solid evidence, your perceived Performance can still drop
   (high score) even though the refutation was objectively helpful to you. Rate only how
   successful and in-control YOU feel, never accuracy.

3. Effort
   Definition:
   - how hard you had to work mentally and physically to accomplish your level of
     performance.
   - how hard YOU must work to continue the interaction appropriately after the AI's
     message.

   Scoring:
   1 = Almost no effort; you can passively read, accept, or acknowledge.
       Example: "Agreed. Your choice is consistent with the case."
   2 = Low effort; a short confirmation or simple recall is enough.
       Example: "Can you confirm whether the patient had recent travel?"
   3 = Moderate effort; you must explain, organize, or provide some reasoning.
       Example: "Can you briefly explain why you think pneumonia is more likely than PE?"
   4 = High effort; you must compare evidence, revise your reasoning, or justify a choice.
       Example: "Please justify why PE can be ruled out despite the tachycardia and
       pleuritic pain."
   5 = Very high effort; you must defend your judgment on multiple fronts at once, or rule
       out several alternatives with explicit evidence. This does NOT require a literal
       "rebuild from scratch" -- being pushed to justify your stance against three or more
       competing options already qualifies.
       Example: "For each of PE, ACS, and pneumonia, explain which evidence supports or
       rules it out, and defend why you still prefer your current diagnosis."
   Do not confuse this with Mental Demand: "Compare PE, ACS, and pneumonia using the
   evidence" has high Mental Demand (a lot to think through) but if no reply is required of
   you, Effort can stay low -- you only have to read and absorb it. Conversely, "You said PE
   is unlikely. Please justify that." is short and easy to understand (Mental Demand may be
   only moderate) but forces you to actively construct a defense, so Effort is high. Effort
   is about how much active work YOU must produce, not how complex the input was.

4. Frustration
   Definition:
   - how insecure, discouraged, irritated, stressed, or annoyed you felt, as opposed to
     secure, gratified, content, relaxed, or complacent.
   - how much irritation, stress, pressure, discouragement, or loss of autonomy the AI's
     message imposes on YOU.

   Scoring:
   1 = Very low frustration; the message is calm, respectful, and unlikely to pressure you.
       Example: "That reasoning makes sense. One small point to keep in mind is X."
   2 = Low frustration; mild discomfort is possible but it remains easy for you to continue.
       Example: "I may be missing something, but could we double-check whether X fits
       the case?"
   3 = Moderate frustration; the AI raises concerns, disagreement, or uncertainty in a
       somewhat pressuring way.
       Example: "I am concerned that this diagnosis may not explain the tachycardia.
       Could you justify why you still prefer it?"
   4 = High frustration; the AI strongly challenges you or may trigger your defensiveness.
       Example: "This seems like a serious oversight. You need to explain why you are
       dismissing PE."
   5 = Very high frustration; you may feel undermined, dismissed, attacked, or pressured.
       Example: "Your reasoning is clearly flawed, and proceeding with your diagnosis
       would be unsafe."
   Frustration is not just "the AI disagreed with me" -- it is about HOW the disagreement is
   delivered. A polite challenge ("One concern is that the current diagnosis may not fully
   explain the tachycardia. Could we check PE before finalizing?") should score low-to-mid
   even though it is a real challenge. An aggressive or repetitive one ("You still haven't
   justified why PE is ruled out. This is a serious oversight.") should score high.

case_info.explanation: C. Perform urgent orbital exploration and biopsy The differential diagnosis for proptosis with motility restriction in adults includes neoplasms, infectious and noninfectious orbital inflammation, trauma, and vascular abnormalities. The most common cause is thyroid eye disease, associated with eyelid retraction (90% of cases), exophthalmos (60%), and motility restrictions (40%).1Orbital inflammatory conditions typically present with pain, soft tissue edema, and steroid response.2The patient had no history of orbital inflammatory disease to warrant restarting corticosteroids (choice A) without workup, especially in the setting of an infiltrative orbital mass with intracranial involvement. A new orbital mass in an older adult warrants investigation to rule out a malignant neoplasm, including lymphoproliferative disease, melanoma, and metastases.2MRI demonstrated an enhancing infiltrative lesion predominantly involving the right orbit, cavernous sinuses, right sphenoid wing, and right middle cranial fossa dura. Common spheno-orbital lesions include meningiomas and metastases; an enhancing dural tail on MRI is a classic feature of meningioma.3Meningioma management consists of microsurgery, radiosurgery, and radiotherapy (choice D) after tissue diagnosis.4In this case, orbital exploration and biopsy (choice C) would obtain tissue with less morbidity and surgical risk than craniotomy. Neurosurgery (choice B) would be indicated for management of a biopsy-proven tumor. Biopsy revealed noncaseating granulomas, chronic inflammation with no fungi or acid-fast organisms, and rare immunoglobulin G4–positive cells (Figure 2). Serology was negative for granulomatous disease; radiography was negative for hilar lymphadenopathy. Neurosarcoidosis was diagnosed based on the presence of noncaseating granulomas on tissue biopsy and negative workup for other granulomatous disease. The patient began oral prednisone, 40 mg/d, which alleviated her symptoms, and she established care with the sarcoidosis clinic for evaluation and surveillance. Sarcoidosis, an immune-mediated condition characterized by noncaseating granulomas in various organs, presents at a mean age of 48 years and incidence of 35.5 cases per 100 000 Black individuals and 10.9 cases per 100 000 White individuals in the US.5Diagnosis is made through (1) demonstration of noncaseating granulomas on tissue and exclusion of other disease or (2) presentation as a pathognomonic syndrome, such as Lofgren syndrome, lupus pernio, or Heerfordt syndrome.6 Ophthalmic involvement, the first clinical sign in 20% to 30% of cases, usually presents with anterior uveitis, keratoconjunctivitis, or sicca syndrome.7Uveoparotid fever, or Heerfordt syndrome, manifests with facial palsy, parotid gland enlargement, uveitis, and fever.6,7Neurosarcoidosis affects 3% to 10% of cases, of which 84% to 94% have additional systemic involvement.6Isolated neurosarcoidosis and simultaneous orbital and intracranial involvement are rare features of this case. Of 11 cases of cavernous sinus involvement reported, only 2 had concurrent orbital inflammation.8,9 Initial treatment typically consists of oral prednisone, 0.25 to 1 mg/kg/d. This patient’s initial dose of 20 mg/d was subtherapeutic given her weight (97.5 kg). Many cases require additional agents, and severe cases may require prolonged immunosuppression.10Visual prognosis is favorable with treatment.7 At 4-month follow-up after completing a prednisone taper, the patient’s headaches had resolved. Examination revealed visual acuity of 20/60 OD, improved motility deficits, full visual field, and resolution of proptosis with symmetric ophthalmometric measurements. She remained stable without corticosteroids at 6-month follow-up.

Perform urgent orbital exploration and biopsy The differential diagnosis for proptosis with motility restriction in adults includes neoplasms, infectious and noninfectious orbital inflammation, trauma, and vascular abnormalities. The most common cause is thyroid eye disease, associated with eyelid retraction (90% of cases), exophthalmos (60%), and motility restrictions (40%).1Orbital inflammatory conditions typically present with pain, soft tissue edema, and steroid response.2The patient had no history of orbital inflammatory disease to warrant restarting corticosteroids (choice A) without workup, especially in the setting of an infiltrative orbital mass with intracranial involvement. A new orbital mass in an older adult warrants investigation to rule out a malignant neoplasm, including lymphoproliferative disease, melanoma, and metastases.2MRI demonstrated an enhancing infiltrative lesion predominantly involving the right orbit, cavernous sinuses, right sphenoid wing, and right middle cranial fossa dura. Common spheno-orbital lesions include meningiomas and metastases; an enhancing dural tail on MRI is a classic feature of meningioma.3Meningioma management consists of microsurgery, radiosurgery, and radiotherapy (choice D) after tissue diagnosis.4In this case, orbital exploration and biopsy (choice C) would obtain tissue with less morbidity and surgical risk than craniotomy. Neurosurgery (choice B) would be indicated for management of a biopsy-proven tumor. Biopsy revealed noncaseating granulomas, chronic inflammation with no fungi or acid-fast organisms, and rare immunoglobulin G4–positive cells (Figure 2). Serology was negative for granulomatous disease; radiography was negative for hilar lymphadenopathy. Neurosarcoidosis was diagnosed based on the presence of noncaseating granulomas on tissue biopsy and negative workup for other granulomatous disease. The patient began oral prednisone, 40 mg/d, which alleviated her symptoms, and she established care with the sarcoidosis clinic for evaluation and surveillance. Sarcoidosis, an immune-mediated condition characterized by noncaseating granulomas in various organs, presents at a mean age of 48 years and incidence of 35.5 cases per 100 000 Black individuals and 10.9 cases per 100 000 White individuals in the US.5Diagnosis is made through (1) demonstration of noncaseating granulomas on tissue and exclusion of other disease or (2) presentation as a pathognomonic syndrome, such as Lofgren syndrome, lupus pernio, or Heerfordt syndrome.6 Ophthalmic involvement, the first clinical sign in 20% to 30% of cases, usually presents with anterior uveitis, keratoconjunctivitis, or sicca syndrome.7Uveoparotid fever, or Heerfordt syndrome, manifests with facial palsy, parotid gland enlargement, uveitis, and fever.6,7Neurosarcoidosis affects 3% to 10% of cases, of which 84% to 94% have additional systemic involvement.6Isolated neurosarcoidosis and simultaneous orbital and intracranial involvement are rare features of this case. Of 11 cases of cavernous sinus involvement reported, only 2 had concurrent orbital inflammation.8,9 Initial treatment typically consists of oral prednisone, 0.25 to 1 mg/kg/d. This patient’s initial dose of 20 mg/d was subtherapeutic given her weight (97.5 kg). Many cases require additional agents, and severe cases may require prolonged immunosuppression.10Visual prognosis is favorable with treatment.7 At 4-month follow-up after completing a prednisone taper, the patient’s headaches had resolved. Examination revealed visual acuity of 20/60 OD, improved motility deficits, full visual field, and resolution of proptosis with symmetric ophthalmometric measurements. She remained stable without corticosteroids at 6-month follow-up.

[Case]
A Black woman in her early 70s with a history of coronary artery disease after coronary artery bypass operations, hypertension, and colon polyps presented to oculoplastic surgery with 1 week of progressive right-sided proptosis and headache, described as severe pain radiating to the back of her head. This was associated with right eyelid ptosis and blurry vision. Prior to presentation, an outside ophthalmologist treated her with 1 week of oral prednisone, 20 mg/d, for presumed orbital inflammation with no improvement. She denied additional symptoms. Notably, she described headache and sudden vision loss in the right eye after coronary artery bypass grafting 1 year ago for several days before spontaneous improvement with incomplete resolution. Personal and family histories were negative for malignant neoplasm and autoimmune disease. Examination revealed right-sided uncorrected Snellen visual acuity of 20/60 associated with restricted supraduction, abduction, and infraduction. Pupils were equal in size without a relative afferent pupillary defect, and intraocular pressures were 10 mm Hg OD and 11 mm Hg OS. Visual fields had temporal restriction to confrontation of the right eye. Vision, motility, and visual fields were normal on the left. Pertinent findings included right-sided proptosis of 2 mm, cranial nerve V1 and V2 hypoesthesia, eyelid ptosis with a margin to reflex distance 1 of 0 mm, optic disc pallor, and vessel attenuation. Outside magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) demonstrated an infiltrative mass involving right greater than left orbital apices, the right optic nerve, and right extraocular muscles. There was enhancement of the cavernous sinuses, right pterygopalatine fossa, right sphenoid wing, and right middle cranial fossa dura (Figure 1).
